The large variability of seismic hazard must be considered in design scenarios with a high degree of consequences to failure. The hazard curves (AEP) has been obtained for seven fractiles (5%, 10%, 16%, 50%, 84%, 90% and 5%) that allow estimating the variability of seismic hazard for a given service level. Assuming a log-normal distribution $ln(X) \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_{lnX},\,\sigma_{lnX}^{2})$ for the seismic intensities of a given service level, the dispersion between the 16% and 84% percentiles allows estimating the standard error of the hazard model, according to $\sigma_{lnX} \approx 1/2 \ log ({X_{84\%}}/{X_{16\%}})$ and the mean value $\mu_{lnX} \approx \frac{1}{2} \left( log(X_{84\%}) + log(X_{16\%}) \right)$. 

If $\eta_X=exp(\mu_{lnX})$ is the median (50%) of some seismic intensity measure, the 84% percentile of this measure can be estimated from $X_{84\%} \approx \eta_X \ exp(\sigma_{lnX})$ and this expression can be used to estimate the variability of any seismic design parameter based on that intensity measure, assuming that they have a log-normal distribution and an approximately linear relationship with the seismic intensity. The following table presents the standard error $\sigma_{X}=exp(\sigma_{lnX})$ for different service levels (return periods), based on 16% and 84% estimates for $S_a(T_n)$ 



The error term $\varepsilon_F$ from [@Stewart2017] is a log-normal random variable, with mean $E[\varepsilon]\approx 0$ and variance $\mathrm{Var}[\varepsilon]\approx \sigma_F^2$. Because the spectral ordinates in rock are actually random variables, with conditional expectation $s_a(T_n)$ and variance $\sigma_A^2$, the error term from this model has been adapted to incorporate the seismic hazard's uncertainty:

$$\mathrm{Var}[\varepsilon_F]\approx \sigma_F^2+\sigma_{A}^2$$


The peak-ground velocity $PGV$ can be explained in terms of its conditional median $\eta_{PGV}(a_*)$ and a random variable $\varepsilon_{V}$ with unit mean $E[\varepsilon_{PGV}]\approx 1$ and constant variance $var[\varepsilon_{PGV}]\approx \sigma_{lnPGV}^2+\sigma_{lnSa}^2$ [^X1]. 

$$PGV\approx pgv^o \ \varepsilon_{V}$$ {#eq-PGVeps}


As a random variable, Arias intensity has also a conditional mean$\eta_{A}(a_*)$ and an error term  $\varepsilon_{A}$ with unit mean $E[\varepsilon_{A}]\approx 1$ and constant variance $var[\varepsilon_{A}]\approx \sigma_{lnAI}^2+\sigma_{lnSa}^2$ 

$$AI \approx ai(pga^o) \ \varepsilon_{A}$$ {#eq-AIeps}


La intensidad de Arias para un cuantil $q$ puede obtenerse mediante 

$$AI_q \approx \eta_{A}(pga^o) \ exp[\Phi_{\varepsilon}^{-1}(q,\sigma)]$$ {#eq-AIq}

donde $\sigma = \sigma_{lnAI}$ es el término de error del modelo de regresión

The reliability $\beta_q \approx exp[\Phi_{\varepsilon}^{-1}(q,\sigma)]$ for the target probability $q$ where $\sigma = \sigma_{LnAI}$ is the error term from the regression model
